generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, these values are not abstract ideals but everyday practice. Honesty means being clear about which ideas are your own and which you have taken from others. Trust means a reader can rely on your citations leading to real sources that say what you claim. Responsibility means owning the conclusions you draw from what you have read. Referencing is where these values become visible on the page, which is why every discipline treats it seriously.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students preparing the same point from the same reading for an essay.

{{learner-a}} likes an idea from the reading, rephrases it, and builds a paragraph around it without naming where it came from. Nothing is copied word for word, so it feels safe. But the reader is left to assume the thinking is {{learner-a}}'s own. The omission is not a formatting slip; it quietly breaks the honesty and trust that academic writing depends on.

{{learner-b}} uses the same idea but attributes it to its author, then adds a line about what the source does and does not establish. The reference is not defensive cover; it is {{learner-b}} being honest about the debt, respectful of the author, and responsible for the further claim. The paragraph is stronger for it, because the reader can see exactly where {{learner-b}}'s own contribution begins.

Both students used the idea well. Only {{learner-b}} treated referencing as an expression of the values, rather than a rule to be managed.
generatedProse.summary: Academic integrity is best understood not as a rulebook but as a set of shared values: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. Referencing is one visible expression of those values rather than a hoop to clear. You can now articulate what integrity means, explain how a value shows up in real academic work, and appraise a difficult situation against the values. The next lesson turns to why referencing in particular matters so much.

check.body: In the worked example, what was the real problem with {{learner-a}}'s paragraph?

items.text: By not attributing the idea, {{learner-a}} let the reader assume borrowed thinking was their own, breaking honesty and trust.
{{learner-a}} rephrased the idea instead of quoting it directly.
{{learner-a}} used an idea from a reading rather than from a published study.
{{learner-a}} added a line about what the idea established.

feedback.correct: That's right. The breach was in letting borrowed thinking pass as one's own, which is where honesty and trust give way.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reader was left to assume, and which values that affects.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The problem was that the idea went unattributed, so the reader assumed the thinking was {{learner-a}}'s own. That breaks honesty and trust, whatever the formatting looks like.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
